title: Fibonacci Number
summary: Return F(n), where F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1 and F(n) = F(n − 1) + F(n − 2).
statement:
The Fibonacci numbers are defined by `F(0) = 0`, `F(1) = 1` and `F(n) = F(n − 1) + F(n − 2)` for `n > 1`. Return `F(n)`.

The plain recursive definition recomputes the same values exponentially many times. This problem is about avoiding that.
hints: Draw the recursion tree for F(5). Which calls repeat?
Memoise: store each F(i) the first time you compute it. Or build the values bottom-up from F(0) and F(1).
You only ever need the last two values, so two variables are enough: O(n) time, O(1) space.
explain: F(2) = F(1) + F(0) = 1 + 0 = 1, so the answer is 1.

title: Climbing Stairs
summary: You climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. Return how many distinct ways reach the top of n steps.
statement:
A staircase has `n` steps. Each time you can climb either 1 or 2 steps. Return the number of distinct ways to reach the top.

Two ways are different if the sequence of step sizes differs.

For example 3 steps can be climbed as 1 + 1 + 1, 1 + 2 or 2 + 1: 3 ways. In general the number of ways to reach step `n` is the sum of the ways to reach steps `n − 1` and `n − 2`.
hints: Your last move onto step n was either a 1-step from n − 1 or a 2-step from n − 2.
So ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2), with ways(1) = 1 and ways(2) = 2.
It is the Fibonacci sequence shifted by one: keep two variables and iterate.
explain: With 2 steps you can climb 1 + 1 or take both at once (2), so there are 2 ways.

title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
summary: Stepping on stair i costs cost[i]; from there you climb 1 or 2 stairs. Starting at stair 0 or 1, return the least cost to get past the last stair.
statement:
`cost[i]` is the cost of stepping on stair `i`. After paying for a stair you may climb one or two stairs. You can start on stair `0` or stair `1` for free (you pay only when you step on a stair).

Return the minimum cost to reach the top, which is the position just past the last stair.
hints: Let best[i] be the minimum cost to stand on stair i (including paying cost[i]).
best[i] = cost[i] + min(best[i − 1], best[i − 2]), with best[0] = cost[0] and best[1] = cost[1].
The top can be reached from either of the last two stairs, so the answer is min(best[n − 1], best[n − 2]). Two variables suffice.
explain: Start on step 1 (cost 15) and climb two steps straight past the top. Paying 15 is the cheapest route, so the answer is 15.

title: N-th Tribonacci Number
statement:
The Tribonacci sequence is defined by `T(0) = 0`, `T(1) = 1`, `T(2) = 1` and `T(n) = T(n − 1) + T(n − 2) + T(n − 3)` for `n ≥ 3`. Return `T(n)`.

The answer fits in a 32-bit integer.

Each term is the sum of the three before it: 0, 1, 1, 2, 4, 7, 13, … . Keeping only the last three values is enough.
hints: Like Fibonacci, but each value depends on the previous three.
Build the values bottom-up instead of recursing.
Keep three variables and shift them along: O(n) time, O(1) space.
explain: T(3) = 0 + 1 + 1 = 2 and T(4) = 1 + 1 + 2 = 4, so the answer is 4.
